title: Exploring Legal Tech Innovations at ILTA Evolve 2025 with Josh Smith and Ken Jones
author: Josh Smith · Ken Jones

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship, leverage or partner-succession routes. It instead focuses on AI-related cybersecurity risks and brief awareness training, with only a limited overlap around accommodating training within billable-time pressures.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation and human control. It offers only a tentative, undeveloped analogy between AI legislation and GDPR, consistent with the cluster’s caution about prediction-heavy evidence but insufficient to establish support or opposition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Legal AI discussions shift from hype to practical implementation
kp.d: Smith characterises the change from 2024 to 2025 as a move from theoretical possibilities toward actual applications, cost savings and workload shifts. Jones similarly emphasises learning what works and what does not through law-firm partnerships with AI providers. These are practitioner observations and conference priorities, not measured findings about adoption or savings.
qs: now I think this year we’re seeing a shift to the practical aspect of it, right? So what are we actually doing with AI? Where is it making a difference?
member firms with leading AI providers and talking about what works and what doesn’t work so that members have something successful that they can bring back to their firms.

kp.k: Confidentiality and governance should guide legal AI deployment
kp.d: Jones identifies governance, control and appropriate use as central implementation concerns. He references ABA Formal Opinion 512 and ISO 42001, qualifying both identifiers with 'I believe', and calls for attention to when firms should use public AI, domain-specific models or AI embedded in legal technology products. His discussion identifies considerations rather than explaining particular legal obligations.
qs: Another really important element, Greg, Marlene, Josh, is the topic of governance, control, the proper use of the technology.
The ABA has formal opinion 512, I believe, that starts to speak to how it’s used.
There are ISO certification standards, ISO 42001 I believe, that’ll be explored at the conference.

how to be very concerned in a world where privacy and confidentiality of client data is important, where to use public AI, where to use domain specific LLMs within a law firm, where to use technology that’s embedded within key legal tech vendors

kp.k: AI increases cybersecurity attack capabilities and defensive demands
kp.d: Host Lambert reports hearing that networks face large increases in attacks and frames AI as enabling automation and enhancement; no attack statistics are supplied. Smith identifies more convincing multilingual attack emails, automation and coding assistance as mechanisms. Jones argues that AI can also help defenders analyse increasing log volumes, detect anomalous behaviour and respond quickly.
qs: I’m hearing that a lot of networks are seeing huge increases in cybersecurity attacks every day.
even from making the email sound more realistic, more human or more appropriate in whatever language you deliver the attack in.
The automation of it, like you mentioned, the help with coding to create some some kind of new code that may not exist that you can sneak in.
the more you can automate, you know, looking for anomalous behavior and then really importantly, responding as quickly as humanly possible to shut it down will be of great value.

kp.k: Short AI-generated videos support attorney security awareness training
kp.d: In response to host Gebauer's argument that more convincing attacks require greater user awareness, Smith reports using Synthesia for 60-second AI-generated training videos. He describes that duration as a practical sweet spot for attorneys concerned about billable time, while qualifying the effectiveness of a pointed message as something that may succeed. This is an experience-based account without engagement or learning-outcome measurements.
qs: we actually have a product that we’ve used called Synthesia to deliver AI generated training videos that are like 60 seconds long.
And we found that that’s really the sweet spot for attorneys, right?
And if you can deliver a pointed message in that 60 seconds, you may find some success there.

kp.k: Security copilots could redirect entry-level work rather than eliminate jobs
kp.d: Smith describes a security copilot summarising logs instantly instead of an analyst spending 30 minutes or an hour reviewing logs and systems. He proposes using the released time for higher-level tasks and learning how to act on AI-provided information. His expectation of a continuing human role and preference for redeployment rather than displacement are explicitly beliefs and hopes, not demonstrated employment outcomes or claims about junior lawyers.
qs: I can go into a security copilot and say give me a synopsis of what just happened and it can instantly tell me what just happened without spending 30 minutes or an hour going through all these logs and all these systems
you can have that entry-level security analyst focusing on a higher-level task or broadening their knowledge of what they need to do with information that AI provides.
But I always think you’ll have that human element. And I hope it doesn’t displace the workforce like some folks think.

kp.k: Technology employment may change composition without shrinking overall
kp.d: Host Gebauer reports reading that new technology jobs will outnumber lost ones but questions where those jobs will arise. Jones offers Salesforce and Meta layoffs alongside AI-related hiring as an illustration of changing job types, suggesting total employment might remain stable or rise. The discussion supplies no source, counts or period for these labour-market claims and does not establish a corresponding legal-sector outcome.
qs: was reading that there’s going to be a lot more new kind of technology jobs than the ones that are lost. It’s just a question of sort of where those are going to be.
Salesforce and Meta are both laying off, but also hiring large numbers of aogenic AI workers.
the workplace, the overall numbers might not be going down. They might even be going up, but the type of job will be varying significantly.

kp.k: Hands-on learning connects legal technology providers and users
kp.d: Jones describes four planned workshops using real-life case studies and collaboration between business partners and members, alongside training in experiential learning for session coordinators. Smith encourages interactive questions and dialogue. These are proposed professional-learning methods for the conference, not evidence of resulting competence gains.
qs: we encourage the sessions to be interactive.

there’s four workshops and the workshops are designed to be more hands-on and with partnerships between the business partners and members to go through real life case studies and work on things together

kp.k: AI supports assessment creation and lecture production in education
kp.d: Jones reports using AI at Seton Hall to create tests, assessments and text-to-voice lectures, describing substantial benefits for faculty. This is a personal cross-domain example of task assistance; the transcript does not identify the teaching subject or provide outcome measurements.
qs: I’m a Seton Hall professor, and we use the technology there to create tests and assessments and to create voice, text-to-voice lectures and all types of things that are hugely beneficial to the faculty.

kp.k: Rapid technological change intensifies information governance challenges
kp.d: Looking ahead, Jones argues that growing data volumes and more advanced technology make information governance increasingly critical. He compares AI-related complexity with firms' earlier difficulty tracking data during cloud migration and invokes recently emerging Chinese AI offerings and open-source versus proprietary choices as signs of uncertainty. He recommends examining data locations, processes, workflows and new tools to improve legal professionals' work; this is a prospective judgment rather than a quantified finding.
qs: the more data we have and the more advanced technology we use, think the more information governance is super critical.
It’s really hard, even as law firms went from on-prem to the cloud to figure out what data is stored where and how to manage it. And this takes it up to another level.
there’ll be a tremendous amount of change and it’ll be a challenge to look at where data is stored, look at work processes, look at workflows.

kp.k: AI regulation remains uncertain and internationally consequential
kp.d: Jones identifies bias, hallucination, privacy, confidentiality and intellectual property as regulatory considerations and stresses the difficulty of setting rules. Smith predicts a GDPR-like trajectory in which European AI regulation precedes weaker state-level US versions, while expressing a preference for a national framework to simplify compliance. These are forecasts and policy preferences, not statements that a uniform US regime exists or will certainly emerge.
qs: there’s at least four areas of consideration, bias, hallucination, privacy and confidentiality, and probably intellectual property also.
It’s incredibly challenging to set rules in this space
We’ll see it originate in Europe, right? And then we’ll have some kind of watered down version of it in the different States.

instead of having the individual States have their own, let’s just have one nationwide one where we can not have to open up 13 different books when we develop a program to make sure we’re getting compliance with all the laws.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Smith and Jones describe a move toward practical AI adoption, cybersecurity automation and workforce reassignment, alongside growing governance challenges.
pts.d: Josh Smith (01:28) describes a 2025 shift from theoretical AI possibilities toward practical use, with cost savings and workload redistribution as questions firms are now exploring rather than quantified outcomes. Ken Jones (02:15–02:45) similarly describes movement from hype to use cases. Smith (14:14) says AI can improve the realism and multilingual quality of attack emails and assist attack automation and coding. Jones (16:07) argues that automated anomaly detection and rapid response offer defensive value as security data grows. Smith (17:00) says a security copilot can summarize logs immediately instead of requiring 30–60 minutes of manual examination, potentially freeing entry-level analysts for higher-level work; his preference for redeployment rather than displacement is expressly a hope. Jones (18:07) suggests overall employment could remain stable or increase while job types change, using technology companies rather than law firms as examples. Smith (15:44) reports using Synthesia to produce short security-training videos that attorneys will watch. Jones (24:35) predicts continued technological change will intensify information-governance and workflow-management challenges for law firms. Smith (27:15) predicts AI legislation will follow a GDPR-like trajectory from Europe to US states, while expressing hope for eventual nationwide US rules. In a cross-domain example, Jones (06:52) reports educational uses of AI for assessments and text-to-voice lectures.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of professional experience, internal discussions, illustrative uses and analogies; no systematic study or benchmark is reported.
pts.d: Smith grounds the practical-adoption observation in discussions within ILTA; Jones invokes Gartner’s hype cycle as an interpretive framework, not measured evidence of adoption. Smith’s Synthesia example is a first-person account of a product used by his organization, with a qualitative judgment about attorney engagement but no participation or learning metrics. His security-copilot example supplies an illustrative 30–60-minute comparison without a named test, sample or evaluation method. Jones’s educational examples draw on his work as a Seton Hall professor. The cybersecurity attack and defense claims are professional assessments without incident counts or measured effectiveness. Jones cites concurrent layoffs and hiring at Salesforce and Meta to illustrate changing job composition, without employment figures or evidence establishing the same outcome for legal employment. Jones’s governance argument draws on law firms’ cloud-migration difficulties and rapidly changing AI offerings. Smith’s legislative forecast rests on analogy to GDPR. Jones also references ABA Formal Opinion 512 and ISO 42001 as governance resources, not proof of AI performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The adoption shift is situated in 2025 versus 2024; operational examples are current, while workforce, governance and regulatory forecasts are conditional and largely undated.
pts.d: Smith and Jones frame practical implementation as this year’s development relative to the prior year’s AI hype. Synthesia training, educational content creation and security-copilot functionality are discussed as present uses or capabilities. The claimed training benefit depends on delivering a pointed message within roughly 60 seconds. Analyst redeployment depends on using AI to absorb routine log review and assigning humans higher-level work; Smith does not assert that displacement will be avoided. Jones’s employment statement is explicitly tentative. In response to a question about the next few years, Jones predicts continuing change and governance difficulty as data volume and technological sophistication increase, without specifying milestones. Smith’s regulatory sequence is probabilistic, and nationwide legislation is an aspiration rather than a firm prediction with a deadline. Jones conditions appropriate adoption on governance of client confidentiality, privacy and technology choices.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are law-firm security and governance teams, entry-level analysts, attorneys and clients whose information firms manage.
pts.d: Smith identifies entry-level knowledge workers and security analysts as candidates for reassignment from routine information review to higher-level tasks and learning. Security teams face more sophisticated AI-enabled attacks while potentially benefiting from automated detection and response. Attorneys are the intended audience for concise AI-generated awareness training. Jones identifies law firms and legal professionals as needing to manage data locations, workflows and choices among public AI, domain-specific models and embedded vendor tools. Clients are affected through privacy and confidentiality risks, rather than any demonstrated change in fees or access to legal advice. Compliance professionals face potentially fragmented rules across jurisdictions; Smith favors nationwide rules to simplify program development. Jones’s employment examples concern technology-company workers, and his educational example concerns faculty. The interview does not offer a concrete forecast of lawyer headcount reductions, law-firm staffing shapes, pricing changes or access-to-justice effects.
